lesson.title: The Print Function: Giving Your Program a Voice
lesson.summary: print() is the built-in function that displays text to the screen, giving a running Python program its only ordinary way to communicate results and messages to the person using it.
lesson.body:
Every installation of the Python language, the foundation the Python Language concept establishes, comes with a small set of built-in functions available without any extra setup, and print() is the one used more than any other. Calling print("Hello, world!") sends the text Hello, world! to the screen followed by a new line, giving a silently running program its first way to show what it is doing. Without print or something like it, a program could still perform calculations internally, but a person watching it run would have no way to see the results.

print() accepts more than one piece of information at a time, separated by commas, and automatically joins them with a single space. The call print("Score:", 95) outputs Score: 95. Notice that this works even though one argument is text and the other is a number; print() handles the conversion to text for you, which is a helpful contrast to the strictness of string concatenation with +, where mixing a string and a number without an explicit str() conversion raises an error. print() is more forgiving because converting values to a readable form for display is exactly its job.

Two optional keyword arguments give finer control over the output. sep changes the separator placed between multiple values, so print("a", "b", "c", sep="-") outputs a-b-c instead of the default a b c. end changes what is printed after everything else; by default end is "\n", a newline character, which is why each call to print() normally starts on a fresh line. Setting end="" suppresses that newline, so print("Loading", end=""); print("...") would output Loading... on one line instead of two.

Beyond simply showing final results, print() is the most immediate debugging tool a beginner has. When a program produces the wrong answer, inserting a temporary print() call to display the current value of a variable at a specific point in the code is often the fastest way to see where the logic went wrong, before reaching for more advanced debugging tools. Watching values change across several print() calls is frequently how a confusing bug becomes an obvious one.

It is also worth knowing that print() always converts its arguments to text before displaying them, using rules similar to the built-in str() function, which is why print(95) and print("95") produce visually identical output even though 95 is an integer and "95" is a string underneath. print() itself does not produce a usable value; its job is entirely the side effect of writing to the screen, which is a preview of the distinction between expressions and statements covered later in this chapter.

print() sends information out of a program to the person watching it run, but it has no way to bring information back in. That is the job of the function introduced next, input(), which is almost always used together with print() to build the two-way conversation of a simple interactive program: print() asks or announces, and input() listens for the reply.
